## Overview

- Esophageal varices develop in patients with **portal hypertension**, most commonly secondary to **hepatic cirrhosis**
- Occur most frequently in the **distal esophagus**, may be accompanied by gastric varices
- Rupture → massive upper GI bleeding with **high mortality rate**
- Therapy includes:
  - Pharmacologic
  - Endoscopic
  - Radiologic (TIPS)
  - Surgical strategies

## Overview – Current Context

- **Liver transplantation** has evolved as the definitive therapy for portal hypertension with liver disease
- Far surpasses shunt surgery by volume in current practice
- Many patients are treated **sequentially** with more than one modality
- Surgical shunts are best applied within the context of:
  - Medical management
  - Endoscopic management
  - TIPS
  - Liver transplantation

## Natural History of Esophageal Varices

- Not all varices bleed; not all cirrhotic patients develop varices
- In a series of **819 patients**: 46% with cirrhosis and no bleeding history had esophageal varices by endoscopy
- Varices may **appear, disappear, or change in size** over time
- Serial endoscopy (84 patients, 2 years):
  - 31% without varices → progressed to **large varices**
  - 70% with small varices → varices **enlarged**

## Natural History – Progression & Regression

- **Dagradi study**: Influence of alcohol on varices
  - Variceal length **increased** in 65% who continued alcohol
  - Variceal length **decreased** in 80% who abstained
- **Baker et al.**: Monitored by endoscopy
  - Regress: **25%**
  - Disappear: **32%**
  - Progress: **21%**

## Natural History – Bleeding & Mortality

- Most bleeding episodes occur during the **first 1–2 years** after identification
- Average mortality rates after esophageal variceal bleeding:
  - **23%** at 1 year
  - **34%** at 2 years
  - **58%** at 3 years
- ~1/3 of deaths attributable to upper GI bleeding
- Larger proportion die from **liver failure**
- Mortality directly from variceal hemorrhage: **10%–17%**

## Risk Factors for Hemorrhage & Death

Clinical parameters associated with increased risk:

| Risk Factor | Details |
|---|---|
| Large varices | Size matters |
| Cherry-red spots | High-risk stigmata |
| Concurrent gastric varices | Additional bleeding source |
| CTP classification | Correlates with death |
| Continued alcohol use | Worsens portal pressure |
| Infection | Precipitates bleeding |
| MELD score | Predicts mortality |

## Rebleeding & Mortality After First Bleed

- Rebleeding rates:
  - **30%** within 6 weeks of initial hemorrhage
  - **60%–75%** within 1 year
- Esophageal varices cause ~**16%** of upper GI bleeding admissions
- All-cause mortality within 1 year of initial hemorrhage: **40%–66%**
- Risk of dying ↑ as interval between 1st and 2nd hemorrhage ↓
- If survive **>12 weeks** post-bleed → risk returns to that of never-bled patients

## Rebleeding – Pediatric Considerations

- Risk of mortality **not well characterized** after a first bleed in children with portal hypertension
- First bleed appears to be **only rarely fatal**
- Associated morbidity is **not well characterized**

## Pharmacologic Management – Prophylaxis

**β-Blocker Therapy**

- **Nadolol**: nonselective β-blocker (β₁ + β₂)
  - Reduced bleeding incidence: 35% → **12%**
  - Reduced fatal bleeds: 18% → **10%**
  - No difference in overall mortality
- Supports prophylactic β-blockade to prevent initial variceal hemorrhage

## Pharmacologic Prophylaxis – Carvedilol

- **Carvedilol**: nonselective β-blocker + α₁-blocking effect
- Better at reducing **hepatic venous wedge pressure gradient** compared to nadolol
- Gained interest as **primary prophylaxis** against variceal bleeding

## Pharmacologic Prophylaxis – Nitrates

- **Nitroglycerin**: vasodilator via nitric oxide on vascular smooth muscle
- Decreases portal pressure at high doses
- Animal studies: portal pressure ↓ 13%, systemic BP ↓ 25%
- Lowers portal pressure **less** than systemic pressure
- Nitrates + β-blockade may offer prophylaxis against initial variceal bleed

## Pharmacologic Prophylaxis – Combination Therapy

- RCTs: nonselective β-blockers (propranolol/nadolol) vs. no therapy → reduced risk of first hemorrhage
- **Isosorbide mononitrate + β-blockade**: further reduces portal pressure
- Shown in **3 studies** to reduce first bleed risk vs. β-blockade alone
- Challenges:
  - **Compliance** (especially in alcoholism)
  - Fatigue (β-blocker side effect)
  - Compromised tachycardia response if bleeding occurs

## Acute Variceal Hemorrhage – Vasopressin

- Posterior pituitary hormone → splanchnic arteriolar vasoconstriction
- Reduces portal BP by ~**15%** (IV or intraarterial)
- Optimal dose: **0.3–0.4 U/min IV**
- Complications ↑ at doses 0.5–0.7 U/min (cardiac, mesenteric, cerebral vasoconstriction)
- No tapering needed; stop at therapeutic endpoint
- Controlled study: ~50% stopped bleeding, but **no difference vs. controls**

## Acute Variceal Hemorrhage – Nitroglycerin + Vasopressin

- Nitroglycerin given concurrently with vasopressin to:
  - Reduce systemic vasoconstrictive effects
  - Further reduce portal pressure
- Infusion begins at **40 μg/min**
- Titrated to mean arterial BP of **65–75 mmHg**

## Acute Variceal Hemorrhage – Octreotide & Somatostatin

- Reduce splanchnic, hepatic, and azygos blood flow
- **Advantage over vasopressin**: no myocardial/cerebral vasoconstriction
- Dose: **250 μg/hr** continuous → increase to **500 μg/hr** if bleeding continues
- RCTs: equivocal results vs. vasopressin (similar efficacy)
- **Terlipressin, somatostatin, octreotide**: equivalent when followed by endoscopic treatment
- None FDA-approved for variceal bleeding (commonly used off-label)

## Prevention of Rebleeding – Pharmacologic

- **Propranolol** (Lebrec): reduces rebleeding via:
  - ↓ Cardiac output (β₁)
  - ↑ Splanchnic arteriolar resistance (β₂)
  - ↓ Portal blood flow & azygos collateral flow
- β-blockade **not widely used** in US for rebleeding prevention (EVL preferred)
- **Nadolol + isosorbide mononitrate** more effective than sclerotherapy for rebleeding; fewer complications (16% vs. 37%)
- **PPI infusion** post-EVL: similar to vasoconstrictor for hemostasis, fewer adverse events
- Multimodal pharmacologic therapy plays a **principal role**

## Endoscopic Therapy – Prophylaxis

- Prophylactic sclerotherapy to prevent first hemorrhage:
  - 3 meta-analyses: **2 concluded no benefit**
  - 1 found decreased mortality with polidocanol
- **VA Cooperative Trial** (281 patients):
  - Prematurely closed due to **excess mortality** in sclerotherapy group
  - Sclerotherapy prevented variceal hemorrhage but caused **ulceration-induced bleeding**
  - Effectively **ended prophylactic sclerotherapy** in the US

## Endoscopic Therapy – Acute Hemorrhage

- **King's College Hospital Trial** (1980, 107 patients):
  - Sclerotherapy controlled bleeding in **57%** vs. **25%** medical therapy
  - Follow-up: improved survival with sclerotherapy
- Important caveats:
  - More nonalcoholic than alcoholic patients
  - Relatively mild liver failure (74 CTP A/B; 33 CTP C)
  - More alcoholic/CTP C patients → harder to show survival benefit
- **VA Cooperative Study**: no long-term survival reduction with sclerotherapy

## Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) vs. Sclerotherapy

- EVL developed as alternative → lower risk of ulceration/perforation
- **7 prospective RCTs** compared EVL vs. sclerotherapy:
  - **Equal efficacy** in controlling active bleeding
  - Complications **significantly lower** with EVL
  - Esophageal strictures: **0%** (EVL) vs. **5%–33%** (sclerotherapy)
- Multiband ligating device → no repeated scope reinsertions
- EVL is now the **endoscopic therapy of choice**

## Endoscopic Therapy – Prevention of Rebleeding

- EVL effectively stops acute bleeding, but **rebleeding remains a problem**
- Intermediate (2–5 year) survival **not improved** in many trials
- Confounding variable: **continued alcoholism**
  - Alcohol abstinence ≥6 months, CTP class, AST → independent predictors of survival
- EVL vs. sclerotherapy:
  - Rebleeding ↓ with EVL (3 studies)
  - Mortality ↓ with EVL (3 studies)
- EVL is the **principal therapy** for preventing rebleeding

## Post-Bleed Antibiotic Prophylaxis

- Prophylactic antibiotics after variceal bleeding:
  - **Decrease risk of rebleeding**
  - Superior to reactive antibiotic use
- Recommended regimens:
  - **Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily** × up to 7 days, OR
  - **Norfloxacin 400 mg PO daily** × up to 7 days

## TIPS – Overview & Evolution

- Developed in the **1990s**; use has since expanded
- Treatment of choice for **high-risk variceal bleeding** patients
- Advances in radiology → placement in more complex/high-risk patients
- Technical success rate: **98%**
- 30-day mortality: **<3%**
- CTP class C: rebleeding ↓ from 60–70% to **40–50%**; mortality ↓ from 40% to **20–35%**

## TIPS – New Imaging: ICE Catheter

- **Intracardiac Echocardiography (ICE)** catheter:
  - Positioned inside vein/artery → sagittal view beyond vessel wall
  - **Budd-Chiari** (no hepatic veins): ICE in intrahepatic IVC → guides needle through IVC wall → liver → intrahepatic PV → **DIPS** (Direct Intrahepatic Portacaval Shunt)
  - **Extrahepatic PV occlusion**: ICE visualizes SMV/splenic vein confluence through IVC wall → facilitates **mesocaval shunt** creation

## TIPS – Extrahepatic Shunts & Cone Beam CT

- Newer imaging/instrumentation → extrahepatic splanchnic & systemic veins usable as targets
- Reduces operative time and radiation dose (safer for pregnant, pediatric, operator)
- **Cone Beam CT** in angiographic suites:
  - Uses fluoroscopy data → cross-sectional imaging
  - Adequate for planning safe needle trajectory
  - Ensures percutaneous splenorenal shunt avoids: pancreatic tail, kidney, duodenum, colon

## TIPS – PowerWire & Chronic PV Occlusion

- **PowerWire**: radiofrequency energy heats tip → effortless passage through tissues
  - Used for side-to-side splenorenal shunt: burns through splenic vein + renal vein walls
  - Maintains access while shunt is dilated and stent placed
- **Chronic PV/splenic vein occlusion**:
  - TIPS alone won't lower pressures throughout portal circulation
  - Requires catheter-directed **thrombolysis + thrombectomy** first
  - Balloon angioplasty ± stenting often needed
  - TIPS maintains rapid flow → ensures patency
  - Often performed in preparation for **liver transplantation**

## TIPS – Noncirrhotic & Special Situations

- **Sinistral portal hypertension** (noncirrhotic):
  - Splenic vein thrombolysis/thrombectomy to reestablish flow
  - If fails + favorable anatomy → **percutaneous splenorenal shunt**
  - If unfavorable anatomy → **splenic embolization** (reduce volume, lower bleeding risk)
- **Arterioportal fistula** (noncirrhotic, patent PV):
  - Congenital or posttraumatic
  - Treated with **coil or plug embolization** of feeding artery
- **EUS-guided intrahepatic shunt**: described in swine model (5 animals survived 2 weeks)

## TIPS – Stents & Patency

- Modern stents: **PTFE-covered** (ePTFE)
  - Less need for intervention, less dysfunction, better outcomes
- **Primary patency** (no revision): 56%–75% at 6 years
- **Primary-assisted patency** (after revision): 77%–96% at 6 years
  - Median survival: **42.8 months**
- Surveillance: **Color Doppler US** at 1 and 6 months
- Restenosis/occlusion rate > recurrent symptom rate
- Risk factors for occlusion: intra-stent stenosis, prior splenectomy, hepatic vein shortening

## TIPS – Clinical Applications

- **Prophylaxis**: Not formally studied, but patients with intractable ascites awaiting transplant → TIPS as bridge → lower portal pressure → low bleeding risk
- **Acute hemorrhage**: Effective when medical/EVL fails
  - As primary therapy: may ↓ treatment failure & mortality in high-risk patients
- **Prevention of rebleeding**: Most common use

## Surgical Shunts – Prophylactic Surgery

- Early trials: portacaval shunts vs. medical therapy
  - Bleeding effectively prevented
  - **No survival benefit** → ↑ deaths from accelerated hepatic failure
- Only **1/3** of patients with varices eventually bleed → surgery not justified as prophylaxis
- **Inokuchi et al.**: 112 patients, prospective controlled
  - Bleeding: 19.2% (medical) vs. **0%** (surgical)
  - No survival difference at 2 years
  - Only study supporting prophylactic surgery
  - Note: majority had **posthepatic cirrhosis** with preserved liver function

## Surgical Shunts – Acute Variceal Hemorrhage

- Pharmacologic + endoscopic therapy used **first** at most centers
- Non-responders → referred for **TIPS or surgical shunt**
- Emergency shunts prevent bleeding more effectively than sclerotherapy, but **overall mortality equivalent**
- If nonoperative measures fail → **emergency surgery promptly considered**
- Emergency shunts normalize portal pressure immediately
- Mortality rate: **20%–55%**

## Emergency Shunts – Outcomes & Choice

- High mortality related to:
  - Decompensated liver function
  - Comorbidity at time of acute bleed
- Outcomes correlate with **CTP class and MELD score**, not shunt type
- Liver failure and encephalopathy → proximate causes of death
- **Portacaval shunt**: acceptable emergency choice (rapid, effective decompression)
  - End-to-side: adequate
  - Side-to-side: preferred if **ascites** present
- **Mesocaval / proximal splenorenal**: effective, avoid porta hepatis dissection
- **DSRS**: emergency use in select patients (large patent splenic vein, controlled ascites)

## Surgical Shunts – Prevention of Rebleeding

- More attractive role: **elective setting** to prevent recurrent hemorrhage
- In appropriately selected patients:
  - Substantially ↓ recurrent bleeding risk
  - Maintain stable liver function
  - Obviate repeated endoscopic procedures
- **TIPS vs. DSRS RCT** (non-responders to medical therapy):
  - Rebleeding: DSRS 5.5% vs. TIPS 10.5% (NS)
  - No difference in encephalopathy or survival
  - TIPS required more interventions (non-covered stents)
  - TIPS slightly more cost-effective at 1 year
  - Conclusion: **equal efficacy**

## Shunt Classification

| Type | Mechanism | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Nonselective** | Complete diversion | Full portal decompression |
| **Partially selective** | Partial diversion | Preserve some portal perfusion |
| **Selective** | Compartmentalization | Decompress varices, preserve hepatic portal flow |

- Relative to nonselective: partial/selective aim to **preserve hepatic portal perfusion** and **minimize liver failure & encephalopathy**

## Nonselective Shunts – General Aspects

- **End-to-side portacaval shunt**: prototype nonselective shunt (first experimental shunt in dogs)
- Side-to-side vs. end-to-side: **no significant clinical differences**
- **Interposition mesocaval shunt**: no clinical/hemodynamic differences vs. side-to-side portacaval
  - High graft thrombosis rate
  - Advantage: avoids porta hepatis dissection (good for transplant candidates)
- **Central/proximal splenorenal shunt** with splenectomy: additional option

## Nonselective Shunts – Current Indications

- Emergency shunt for variceal hemorrhage
- Elective shunt with **significant ascites**
- Treatment of **Budd-Chiari syndrome**
- Long-term bridge to hepatic transplantation (when bleeding not controlled by endoscopy or TIPS)

## Budd-Chiari Syndrome – Shunt Considerations

- Ascites, abdominal pain, portal hypertension → **side-to-side portacaval shunt** (TIPS preferred if feasible)
- Side-to-side necessary: PV serves as major **efferent conduit**
- Fulminant disease or cirrhosis → **liver transplantation** preferred
- **Caudate lobe hypertrophy** may prevent side-to-side portacaval shunt → **mesocaval shunt** more feasible
- IVC occlusion → infrahepatic collaterals to azygos → mesocaval shunt decompresses portal circulation
- Mesoatrial shunt: long, poor patency, poor outcomes → generally avoided
- **Long-term anticoagulation** usually necessary
- Must diagnose and treat underlying **hypercoagulable state**

## Distal Splenorenal Shunt (DSRS) – Concept

- Introduced by **Warren et al.**
- Goal: preserve **hepatopetal blood flow** in PV while decompressing varices
- Distal splenic vein → anastomosed to **left renal vein**
- Collaterals ligated (coronary vein, gastroepiploic vein)
- **Compartmentalizes** portal circulation:
  - High-pressure SMV system → perfuses liver
  - Decompressed gastrosplenic system → prevents variceal bleeding

## DSRS – Contraindications & Controversies

- **Contraindicated** in advanced ascites:
  - Lymphatics transected during renal vein dissection
  - Elevated sinusoidal pressures persist
  - May **worsen ascites**
- Preserving hepatic function better than nonselective shunts: **controversial**
- Controlled trials: ↓ portosystemic encephalopathy after DSRS
- Portal flow maintained in **nonalcoholic cirrhosis** and noncirrhotic portal hypertension
- Portal flow rapidly collateralizes in **alcoholic cirrhosis** (especially with continued alcohol)
- Failure to ligate coronary vein → early loss of hepatopetal flow

## DSRS – Pancreatic Siphon & Splenopancreatic Disconnection

- Despite surgical interruption of collaterals → collaterals develop through **pancreatic siphon**
- **Splenopancreatic disconnection** improves selectivity (especially alcoholic cirrhosis)
- However:
  - Technically demanding
  - Frequently bloody (fibrotic pancreas)
  - Clinical benefits **not clearly shown**

## DSRS – Preoperative Requirements

- **Visceral or CT angiography** required before DSRS
- Requires **patent splenic vein**, preferably ≥ **7 mm** diameter
- **Not candidates**:
  - Previous splenectomy
  - Thrombosed splenic vein

## DSRS – Controlled Trials vs. Nonselective Shunts

- **6 of 7** controlled trials evaluated alcoholic cirrhotic patients
- Summarized by **Jin and Rikkers**:
  - **No survival advantage** of either procedure
  - 4/7 trials: **less encephalopathy** after selective shunt
  - 3/7 trials: no difference in encephalopathy
  - Rebleeding rates: **no difference** (one trial: higher after DSRS)

## DSRS vs. Endoscopic Therapy

- Rebleeding **less frequent** with selective shunts
- Hepatic portal perfusion **better maintained** by sclerotherapy
- Encephalopathy rates: **similar**
- Sclerotherapy effectively controls initial bleeding
- Non-responders → **prompt surgery**
- Another surgical indication: **poor access to advanced medical care** (avoids multiple endoscopy visits)

## Partial Shunt (Sarfeh)

- Decompresses varices while **preserving hepatic portal perfusion**
- **8-mm or 10-mm PTFE graft** interposed between PV and IVC
- RCT: partial (8 mm) vs. nonselective (16 mm):
  - **Lower encephalopathy** with partial shunt
  - Similar survival
- **Rosemurgy series** (170 patients):
  - 56% alcoholic, 44% nonalcoholic
  - 38% CTP A/B, 62% CTP C
  - Variceal bleeding after shunt: **2%** (very uncommon)
  - Actual survival superior to MELD-predicted
  - Encouraged for patients **not eligible/suitable for transplant**

## Portacaval Shunt – Technique

- Side-to-side, end-to-side, or interposition graft
- Side-to-side: relieves ascites (↓ intrahepatic sinusoidal pressure) + ↓ portal pressure gradient
- **Current indication**: significant ascites + bleeding varices unresponsive to nonsurgical treatment + **not a transplant candidate**
- Transplant candidates: avoid porta hepatis dissection → prefer DSRS or mesocaval

## Portacaval Shunt – Surgical Steps

1. Transverse upper abdominal incision
2. Encircle and retract common bile duct to patient's left
3. If replaced right hepatic artery from SMA → encircle and retract left
4. Dissect and encircle PV and IVC (between liver edge and right renal vein)
5. Partially occluding clamps on IVC and PV
6. Longitudinal venotomy (~2 cm) in each vein
7. 6-0 polypropylene stay sutures at corners
8. Running anastomosis
9. Remove clamps → check hemostasis

**Figure 83.7**: Completed side-to-side portocaval anastomosis → normalizes portal pressures, hepatofugal flow through shunt

## Mesocaval Shunt – Indications & Technique

- Long-term bridge to transplant or definitive therapy (endoscopic/TIPS failure)
- Conduit: PTFE, Dacron, or **internal jugular vein autograft**
  - Vein graft: better long-term patency
  - Synthetic: more common, avoids jugular harvest morbidity
- Advantage: dissection **away from porta hepatis** (transplant-friendly)
- Disadvantage: long course around duodenum, relatively poor long-term patency

## Mesocaval Shunt – Surgical Steps

1. Transverse upper abdominal incision
2. Elevate transverse colon → identify middle colic vein → SMV
3. Dissect 2–3 cm SMV segment free of tributaries
4. Dissect IVC through right colon mesentery (caudal to duodenum)
5. Shunt should take **straight path** from SMV to IVC (avoid duodenal compression)

## Jugular Vein Conduit – Technique

- **Left neck** preferred (left jugular vein slightly longer)
- Incision along anterior border of sternocleidomastoid
- Divide platysma → identify jugular vein
- Ligate and divide branches
- Dissect from **clavicle to mastoid**
- Ligate proximally and distally with silk → excise graft → place in sterile saline
- Close neck wound
- Proximal end → end-to-side to **SMV** (6-0 polypropylene)
- Distal end → end-to-side to **IVC** (6-0 polypropylene)
- Flow should be **1–2 L/min**; lower → inspect for technical problems

**Figure 83.8**: Left jugular vein provides ideal autologous endothelialized vein graft for mesocaval shunt (8–10 cm graft)

## Meso-Rex Shunt

- For **extrahepatic PV occlusion** without cirrhosis/advanced fibrosis
- Requires: patent intrahepatic **left PV** + patent **SMV** (or suitable collateral)
- Venous conduit from SMV → left PV (usually **left internal jugular vein**)
- **Key advantage**: restores portal blood flow to liver AND relieves portal hypertension
  - Preserves liver integrity and function long term
- More common in **children**; selected adults may benefit
- Surgical dissection follows **round ligament** to left PV
- Recent consensus: advocated for more common application in children with extrahepatic PV occlusion

**Figure 83.9**: Meso-Rex shunt creation – dissection of round ligament to left portal vein, restoring portal inflow via SMV graft

## DSRS – Technical Details

- Transverse upper abdominal incision
- Take down gastrocolic omentum → divide **right gastroepiploic vein**; leave **short gastric veins** intact
- Mobilize splenic flexure caudally
- Retract inferior border of pancreas anteriorly/cranially
- Dissect **splenic vein** free from pancreas → ligate all tributaries
  - Most challenging aspect (especially with pancreatic fibrosis)
- Dissect medially to SMV confluence, laterally for adequate length
- If splenopancreatic disconnection: continue to spleen, ligate all pancreatic tributaries

**Figure 83.10**: Anatomy for DSRS – short gastric veins intact; coronary vein and right gastroepiploic veins ligated

## DSRS – Left Renal Vein & Coronary Vein

- Dissect **left renal vein**; ligate lymphatics (avoid chylous ascites)
- Ligate and divide **left adrenal vein** (mobilization)
- Leave **gonadal vein and lumbar veins** intact (additional outflow)
- If circumaortic left renal vein with small anterior branch → anastomose to IVC (**distal splenocaval shunt**)
- **Coronary vein ligation** is essential for selectivity:
  - Preferably at junction with portal/splenic vein
  - Or at superior border of pancreas
  - Generally large and attenuated
- Shunt flow: **300–1000 mL/min**

**Figure 83.6**: DSRS diagram – ligation of coronary vein, drainage of splenic vein into left renal vein; right gastroepiploic vein ligated

## Minimally Invasive Portosystemic Shunts

- TIPS methodology → minimally invasive shunt creation with improving patency
- RCT: DSRS vs. TIPS → **no superiority of DSRS**
- Many clinicians recommend **TIPS as long-term solution**; reserve surgical shunts when TIPS not feasible
- DSRS placed via **retroperitoneum** or via **left renal vein into splenic vein** (percutaneous)
- As stent techniques/design improve → increasingly attractive alternatives to rare surgical shunts

## Devascularization Procedures – Overview

- Intent: disconnect varices from hypertensive portal system
- **Avoid encephalopathy** by preserving hepatic portal perfusion
- Gold standard: **Sugiura procedure**
  - Thoracic esophageal transection + devascularization
  - Followed weeks later by laparotomy
  - Extensive esophageal + gastric devascularization
  - Preserves coronary vein → azygos collaterals (discourages varix reformation)

## Sugiura Procedure – Outcomes

- **Initial report** (Sugiura & Futagawa, 276 patients):
  - Operative mortality: **4.3%**
  - Varix recurrence: **2.3%** (1–10 year follow-up)
  - 1-year actuarial survival: **83%**
  - Survival by CTP: A=95%, B=87%, C=57%
  - Elective > emergency outcomes
- **Outside Japan**: results not duplicated
- **Orozco et al.**: 10-year experience, one-stage transabdominal → mortality correlated with CTP
- **Toronto (Dagenais)**: 22% operative mortality (emergency); 5-year survival: A=100%, B=43%, C=25%

## Devascularization – Additional Data & Indications

- 32 patients, transabdominal esophagogastric devascularization:
  - 11/12 **without liver disease** survived >10 years
  - 20 with cirrhosis: 5-year survival **51%**
- Effective alternative for **diffuse splanchnic venous thrombosis** without liver disease
- Only RCT (bilharzial cirrhosis): devascularization → longer survival without encephalopathy vs. shunt
- **Indications**: unsuitable PV anatomy, shunt failures, non-responders to medical management
- CTP C → consider **liver transplantation**
- Reserve for rare patients: refractory bleeding + ineligible for TIPS/shunt/transplant

## Liver Transplantation – Definitive Therapy

- Definitive therapy for **advanced liver failure** (CTP B or C)
- Variceal hemorrhage → most common manifestation prompting transplant evaluation
- Acute management: endoscopic diagnosis + EVL + pharmacologic therapy ± TIPS
- Strong correlation between CTP class and long-term outcome → transplant is **treatment of choice** for advanced liver disease
- All other treatments used in **complementary fashion**; sequential application common
- Liver transplantation = ultimate solution for cirrhosis + end-stage liver failure

## Liver Transplantation – Practical Considerations

- Disparity between patients awaiting transplant and donor supply → **unpredictable waiting period**
- Operative morbidity/mortality correlate with **preoperative condition**
  - Use alternative measures to arrest bleeding + optimize condition before transplant
- **Active alcoholics**: precluded from transplant; require ≥**6-month abstinence**
  - May need temporizing alternative therapies
- Liver transplantation → **immediate normalization** of portal pressure

## Liver Transplantation – Shunt Implications

- Portacaval shunt or porta hepatis dissection → makes subsequent transplant **more difficult**
- If transplant anticipated: shunt **outside porta hepatis** preferred
  - **DSRS and mesocaval shunts** preferred
- Surgical shunt may be attractive if transplant not needed for **several years**
- CTP C patients requiring short-term transplant → managed with **TIPS as bridge**
  - TIPS may improve CTP class and reduce pre-transplant morbidity

## Meso-Rex Shunt for PV Occlusion After Transplant

- Especially in **children**: extrahepatic PV thrombosis months/years post-transplant
- Manifestations: portal hypertension, GI bleeding from Roux-en-Y, splenomegaly, encephalopathy
- **Meso-Rex shunt** (SMV → left PV):
  - Placed in **rex recessus** space via round ligament
  - Autologous vein conduit
  - Relieves portal hypertension + restores **physiologic flow** to liver
- Young children: seldom experience life-threatening bleeds; managed medically + planned shunts/transplant

## Extrahepatic Portal Vein Thrombosis – Overview

- Relatively uncommon cause of portal hypertension
- Management **distinctly different** from cirrhosis:
  - Usually **normal liver**
  - Survival not limited by liver disease progression
- Etiology:
  - Direct: neonatal peritonitis, trauma, porta hepatis tumors, congenital PV abnormalities
  - Indirect: neonatal sepsis, dehydration, hypercoagulable states
- Results in **presinusoidal portal hypertension** with hepatopetal collaterals (excellent portal perfusion)

## Extrahepatic PV Thrombosis – Treatment Options

1. **Expectant medical management**:
   - Bleeding generally well tolerated (normal liver)
   - Appropriate in infants (self-limited; 50% outgrow bleeding)
2. **Endoscopic variceal ablation + surgery** (adults):
   - Mortality approaches **20%** over time with recurrent bleeding
   - Normal liver → excellent candidates for aggressive treatment
3. **Acute episode management**: resuscitation → vasopressin/octreotide → endoscopic ablation

## Extrahepatic PV Thrombosis – Surgical Approach

- Recurrent bleeding → **CT angiography/MRA** (portal, mesenteric, splenic veins)
- Spleen in situ + patent splenic vein → **DSRS** (excellent candidate)
  - Central splenorenal or mesocaval shunts also possible if SMV open
- Splenic vein occluded or spleen absent → further endoscopic ablation
  - If fails → exploration
  - Rare: shuntable vein found (e.g., coronary vein → coronary-caval shunt)
  - Most often: **gastric devascularization + splenectomy**
- Recurrent hemorrhage after devascularization: **20%–30%** → further ablation; rarely esophagogastrectomy

## Present Role of Surgical Shunts

- Shunt may serve as **long-term bridge to transplant**
- Vast majority with underlying liver disease → treated with **transplant** if candidates
- Surgical shunts reserved for patients with **good hepatic reserve** and variceal bleeding
- Excellent results in this setting
- Over 25 years: liver transplantation + TIPS have substantially changed management
  - CTP class of shunt patients progressively improved
  - Need for emergency surgery declined
  - Nonselective shunt use declined (EVL, TIPS, transplant)
  - Less risky patients selected for elective shunts
  - Postoperative encephalopathy ↓; long-term (10-year) survival ↑

## Present Role – Pediatric Shunts

- Another role: **children with variceal hemorrhage** after endoscopic therapy
- Excellent results with:
  - **Meso-Rex shunt**
  - **Distal splenorenal shunt**
  - **Mesocaval shunt**
- To prevent bleeding in pediatric portal hypertension

## Algorithm for Definitive Therapy (Figure 83.11)

**Transplant Candidates:**
- Nonalcoholic/abstinent alcoholic cirrhotics
- Good operative risk + controllable ascites + compatible anatomy → **Selective shunt or TIPS**
- Intractable ascites → **TIPS or nonselective shunt**
- Poor operative risk / CTP C → **TIPS** (bridge to transplant)
- Failure of endoscopic therapy → **TIPS**

**Non-Transplant Candidates:**
- Noncirrhotic, active alcoholic, elderly, significant cardiopulmonary disease, noncompliant, poor access, gastric varices
- Compliant + ready access → **Endoscopic therapy**
- Poor access / gastric varices → **Selective shunt or TIPS**
- Splanchnic venous thrombosis → **Devascularization**
- Failure → **Surgery or TIPS**

## Algorithm – Key Decision Points

| Patient Factor | Preferred Approach |
|---|---|
| Transplant candidate, good operative risk | Selective shunt or TIPS |
| Transplant candidate, intractable ascites | TIPS or nonselective shunt |
| CTP class C / progressive disease | TIPS → Transplant |
| Non-transplant, compliant, good access | Endoscopic therapy |
| Non-transplant, poor access / gastric varices | Selective shunt or TIPS |
| Splanchnic venous thrombosis | Devascularization |
| Endoscopic therapy failure | TIPS |

## Summary – Evolution of Management

- Clinical management of bleeding esophageal varices has **changed radically** in 25 years
- Key changes:
  - Improved TIPS patency (ePTFE-covered stents)
  - Minimally invasive intravascular shunt techniques
  - Improved liver transplant outcomes
  - EVL: excellent efficacy, lower complications → increased use
  - TIPS: minimally invasive, successful → reduced need for surgical shunts
  - TIPS increasingly used when endoscopic intervention fails
  - Liver transplantation routinely recommended for advanced liver failure

## Summary – Current Role of Surgical Shunts

1. **Less frequent** than in previous era
2. Emergency setting in adults: only when medical therapy, endoscopic control, or TIPS have **failed**
3. Elective: occasionally useful as **long-term bridge to transplant**
4. Elective: definitive therapy for **noncirrhotic portal hypertension** or **CTP A cirrhosis** if TIPS/intravascular DSRS not feasible
5. Beneficial for **Budd-Chiari syndrome** when TIPS not technically feasible

## Summary – Preferred Shunt

- **Selective DSRS** preferred in patients **without ascites**:
  - Lower risk of portosystemic encephalopathy
  - Potential for preserving portal blood flow
- **Multidisciplinary approach** to evaluation and treatment improves outcomes
- Selective use of each therapy, alone or in combination → improved outcomes
